![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225003/assets/d333ab14f8a42bb1d40894421afc76ff60acbb6c4cb858ddee5f6e8a39be2d15.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\sqrt{1-z}⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of a right circular cylinder of height $1$ whose base is a circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin, as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
question.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\sqrt{1-z}⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of $S$ is parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225003/assets/5193451b39b03b11cf9780fd7039360ba8fb5de5876a3593f7a5dadde2e7be5b.png)

 
Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=1$ for ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 4.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
F(x,y,0)=⟨0,\,0,\,({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\sqrt{1-1}⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 4.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\sqrt{1-z}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\sqrt{1-0}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying a change of variables $(x,y)\to (r,\theta ),\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & =-{∬}_{D}{r}^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-{∬}_{D}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r \\  & =-2\pi \cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =-2\pi \cdot 4 \\  & =-8\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =0+(-8\pi ) \\  & =-8\pi .\end{aligned}
$$
